prompt: `Lendable` declares `String title();` with no modifier written at all. What is the method?
hint: The words are left out because they are implied.

choices.text: Package-private and abstract, since no access word was written
choices.why: In a class that would be package-private; in an interface the default is public.

choices.text: Public and abstract
choices.why: Right: every interface method is both unless it says otherwise.

choices.text: Public, with an empty body that returns `null`
choices.why: There is no body at all; a class that signs must write one.

choices.text: Private to the interface until a class implements it
choices.why: A private interface method needs the word `private` and a body.

prompt: `books.sort(null)` put `Dom Casmurro` first. What told `List.sort` how to order two books?
hint: `null` means "use the elements' own order".

choices.text: The order in which the books were added to the list
choices.why: They were added as `O Guarani`, `Dom Casmurro`, `Iracema`, and came out in another order.

choices.text: `loanDays()`, which every `Lendable` has
choices.why: All three books lend for 21 days; that could not order them.

choices.text: `Book.compareTo`, from `Comparable<Book>`
choices.why: Right: `List.sort` calls the method the contract promises.

choices.text: The hash codes of the `Book` objects
choices.why: Hash codes have no order that means anything here; `compareTo` compares titles.

prompt: What did `javac` say about `Magazine`, which implements `Lendable` and writes only `title()`?
hint: The message names the missing method.

choices.text: That it is not abstract and does not override `loanDays()`
choices.why: Right: sign the contract and you deliver every method, or declare the class abstract.

choices.text: Nothing; `loanDays()` returns 0 by default
choices.why: Abstract methods have no default value; the compiler refuses.

choices.text: That `Lendable` cannot be instantiated
choices.why: That was `Nope`'s error, which tried `new Lendable()`.

prompt: Which of these lines compile, given section 02's `Lendable`, `Book` and `Dvd`? Choose all that apply.
hint: A variable may have an interface type; an object may not.

choices.text: `Lendable item = new Dvd("Central do Brasil");`
choices.why: Yes: `Dvd` signed `Lendable`.

choices.text: `Lendable item = new Lendable();`
choices.why: No: `Lendable is abstract; cannot be instantiated`.

choices.text: `Comparable<Book> c = new Book("Iracema");`
choices.why: Yes: `Book` signed `Comparable<Book>` as well.

choices.text: `Comparable<Book> c = new Dvd("Central do Brasil");`
choices.why: No: `Dvd` signed only `Lendable`.

prompt: A colleague writes a `Map` class next year that implements `Lendable`. Without changing a line of `Desk`, will its loop over a `List<Lendable>` work with maps?
hint: The loop was written against the contract.

choices.text: No, because `Desk` was compiled before `Map` existed
choices.why: Compiling against the interface is exactly what lets later classes fit.

choices.text: Yes, each map answers with its own `title()` and `loanDays()`
choices.why: Right: code written against an interface works with every class that signs it, the later ones included.

choices.text: Only if `Map` also extends `Book`
choices.why: No parent is needed; `Book` and `Dvd` share none either.

choices.text: Only after `Desk` adds a `case` for maps to its loop
choices.why: The loop has no cases; it calls the interface's methods and each object answers.

prompt: `renewable()` was added to `Lendable` as a `default` method. What happened to `Book.java` and `Dvd.java`?
hint: They were copied unchanged.

choices.text: They had to add `renewable()` before they compiled again
choices.why: That is what an abstract method would have demanded; a default one asks nothing.

choices.text: Nothing; they compiled and inherited `true`
choices.why: Right: both answered `renewable` from the default body.

choices.text: They compiled, and `renewable()` threw for them until they wrote it
choices.why: A default has a body that runs; nothing throws.

prompt: How is `describe` called, and why that way?
hint: It is `static`.

choices.text: `item.describe()`, because every implementer inherits it
choices.why: Static interface methods are not inherited; `Book.describe` does not exist.

choices.text: `Book.describe(item)`, because `Book` is the class that implements it
choices.why: Not inherited, so not reachable through `Book`.

choices.text: `Lendable.describe(item)`, because a static method belongs to the interface
choices.why: Right: it is called on the interface's name, as `Shelf` did.

prompt: `javap Lendable` listed the methods the interface shows the world. How many lines of methods did it print?
hint: Count the abstract, default and static ones; the private one is missing.

prompt: Two default methods in an interface both need to update a count of how many items were lent. Following the section, what does the design want?
hint: What can an interface hold, and what can it not?

choices.text: A non-final field in the interface
choices.why: An interface may declare constants only; it has no fields that change.

choices.text: A private default method that keeps the count
choices.why: A method cannot keep a value between calls without a field to put it in.

choices.text: An abstract class
choices.why: Right: shared state and the code around it belong to an abstract class, lesson 21's tool.

choices.text: A second interface whose default method holds the number
choices.why: Interfaces hold no state, however many there are.

prompt: `Audiobook implements Printed, Recorded` and writes no `label()`. What happens?
hint: The compiler refuses to guess.

choices.text: `Printed`'s label runs, because it is listed first
choices.why: No order of `implements` decides it.

choices.text: Both labels run, one after the other
choices.why: One call runs one method.

choices.text: It does not compile: it inherits unrelated defaults for `label()`
choices.why: Right: the class has to write its own `label()`.

prompt: Inside `Audiobook`, the call that runs the default from `Recorded` is written `Recorded.___.label()`.
hint: The same word that reaches a parent class's method.

prompt: `Leaflet extends Catalogue implements Printed`. Both give a `label()`. Which one runs, and why does the rule exist?
hint: It printed `a catalogue entry`.

choices.text: `Printed`'s, since interfaces are newer than classes
choices.why: The class's method won, and the opposite rule would let old classes change.

choices.text: `Catalogue`'s, so that adding a default cannot change an existing class
choices.why: Right: a class that already had the method keeps it.

choices.text: Neither; it is the same compile error as `Audiobook`
choices.why: A class against an interface is not a clash; only two interfaces are.

choices.text: Whichever was compiled last
choices.why: Compilation order never decides which method runs.

prompt: A class implements `Printed` only, and wants `Recorded`'s label too. Can it write `Recorded.super.label()`?
hint: The last sentence about `.super` in section 04.

choices.text: Yes, any interface's default can be reached that way
choices.why: Only an interface the class names in its own `implements`.

choices.text: No: that form reaches only interfaces the class signs directly
choices.why: Right: it reaches a direct superinterface, and `Recorded` is not one.

choices.text: Yes, as long as `Recorded` is in the same directory
choices.why: Location is not the rule; the `implements` clause is.

prompt: What does `sealed interface Item permits Book, Dvd` say?
hint: Read `permits` literally.

choices.text: That only `Book` and `Dvd` may implement `Item`
choices.why: Right: the list is enforced by the compiler.

choices.text: That `Book` and `Dvd` may not be extended by anything
choices.why: Each permitted class decides that itself, with `final`, `sealed` or `non-sealed`.

choices.text: That `Item` can be implemented in this file and no other
choices.why: The permitted classes were in their own files.

prompt: `public class Dvd implements Item` was refused with `sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected`. What is the compiler asking?
hint: A permitted class must say what happens below it.

choices.text: To add `Dvd` to `permits`
choices.why: It was already there; that was not the complaint.

choices.text: To declare what is allowed below `Dvd`
choices.why: Right: `final` closes it, `sealed` lists its own, `non-sealed` opens it again.

choices.text: To mark `title()` as `final` so no subclass changes it
choices.why: The message is about the class's modifiers, not a method's.

choices.text: To make `Item` an abstract class instead of an interface
choices.why: Sealed interfaces are allowed; the fix was one word on `Dvd`.

prompt: Match each modifier on a permitted class to what it means for classes below it.
hint: Section 05's three words.

pairs.right: Only the classes in its own `permits` may extend it
Any class may extend it again

right_distractors: Only classes in the same file may extend it

prompt: Somebody adds `Magazine` to `Item`'s `permits` and writes the class. What happens to `Rules.loanDays`, whose switch has no `default`?
hint: The compiler read `permits` to accept the switch.

choices.text: It returns 0 for magazines
choices.why: No case covers them, and there is no default value to fall back on.

choices.text: It throws at run time the first time a magazine arrives
choices.why: The failure comes earlier than that, which is the point.

choices.text: The code no longer compiles: the switch is missing a case
choices.why: Right: every switch over `Item` must decide the new kind before the code builds.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the switch only names `Book` and `Dvd`
choices.why: Naming two out of three is exactly what makes it incomplete.

prompt: Put the steps of growing the `Lendable` contract by `renewable()` in the order the lesson took them.
hint: Write the default first; the old classes need nothing.
items: Add `default boolean renewable()` with a body to `Lendable`
Override `renewable()` in `Game`, the one class that disagrees

prompt: Your team needs a type for payment methods: card, Pix and boleto, each with different rules, and no other kind may ever be accepted without review. What do you write?
hint: Which tool lists the implementers and lets a switch know it is complete?

choices.text: An ordinary interface, and a `default` branch in every switch
choices.why: Any new class would slip in and take the default silently.

choices.text: A sealed interface that permits the three
choices.why: Right: adding a fourth means editing `permits`, and every switch then fails until it decides.

choices.text: Three unrelated classes with a `type` string field each
choices.why: A string is checked by nothing; a typo becomes a new kind.

choices.text: An interface with three default methods, one per kind of payment
choices.why: Defaults share behaviour; they do not limit who may implement.

prompt: Which statement about Java's inheritance does the lesson end on?
hint: One class, several interfaces.

choices.text: Behaviour and state both arrive from any number of parents
choices.why: State arrives from one class only.

choices.text: Interfaces carry state, classes carry behaviour
choices.why: The other way round: interfaces hold no state.

choices.text: Behaviour from several interfaces, state from one class
choices.why: Right: and where two answers compete with no rule, you write the answer down.
